evidence:
IoT sensors: 50k events/sec,
sub-second latency needed,
multiple consumers.
scenarios.hint: Which service is built for high-throughput ordered event streams with multiple consumers?
scenarios.situation: 50k IoT events/sec need sub-second ingestion with multiple consumers reading the same stream.
scenarios.title: Fifty thousand events a second
scenarios.why: Kinesis Data Streams provides ordered, replayable, high-throughput streaming with multiple consumers per shard. SQS is queue-based (not replayable multi-consumer streaming); S3 batch uploads aren't sub-second; RDS isn't an ingestion service.

choices: Kinesis Data Streams with custom consumers
evidence:
Clickstream: 20k events/sec.
Need: land in S3 as Parquet,
near-real-time, zero consumer code.
scenarios.hint: Which service loads streaming data to destinations with no consumer code?
scenarios.prompt: Which service delivers with zero consumer code?
scenarios.situation: Clickstream at 20k events/sec must land in S3 as Parquet near-real-time with no custom consumer code.
scenarios.title: No consumer code required
scenarios.why: Kinesis Data Firehose is the managed delivery service: it buffers, converts (e.g., to Parquet), and loads streaming data into S3 and other destinations with no consumer code. Data Streams and MSK require consumers; DynamoDB direct PUT isn't a streaming pipeline.

evidence:
Team knows Kafka deeply.
Need: Kafka API compatibility,
long retention, exactly-once
semantics.
scenarios.hint: Which AWS service is Kafka-compatible and managed?
scenarios.prompt: Which service fits the Kafka team?
scenarios.situation: A team with deep Kafka expertise needs Kafka API compatibility, long retention, and exactly-once semantics on AWS.
scenarios.title: Kafka, managed
scenarios.why: Amazon MSK provides managed Apache Kafka with Kafka API compatibility, configurable long retention, and exactly-once semantics support. Firehose/Data Streams aren't Kafka-compatible; SQS FIFO lacks Kafka's log semantics and retention model.

evidence:
On-prem Oracle -> Aurora PostgreSQL.
Need: minimal downtime, continuous
replication until cutover.
scenarios.hint: Which service replicates databases continuously with minimal downtime?
scenarios.prompt: Which service migrates with minimal downtime?
scenarios.situation: An on-prem Oracle database must migrate to Aurora PostgreSQL with minimal downtime and continuous replication until cutover.
scenarios.title: Moving Oracle without stopping
scenarios.why: DMS performs full-load plus change-data-capture replication, keeping the target in sync until cutover for minimal downtime. Manual uploads can't do CDC; rewriting the app is unnecessary; screenshots aren't a migration strategy.

evidence:
Partners send nightly CSVs via SFTP.
Need: land in S3, keep the SFTP
interface, managed service.
scenarios.hint: Which managed service speaks SFTP/S3 natively?
scenarios.prompt: Which service keeps the SFTP interface?
scenarios.situation: Partners send nightly CSVs via SFTP; the files must land in S3 while keeping the SFTP interface as a managed service.
scenarios.title: SFTP, but it lands in S3
scenarios.why: AWS Transfer Family provides managed SFTP/FTPS/FTP endpoints backed by S3 — partners keep their workflow, files land in S3. The streaming services don't speak SFTP; they're for event streams, not file transfers.

evidence:
Files land in S3 unpredictably.
Need: trigger processing within
seconds of arrival.
scenarios.hint: Which S3 feature pushes events on object creation?
scenarios.situation: Files land in S3 unpredictably; processing must trigger within seconds of arrival.
scenarios.title: The file just landed — go
scenarios.why: S3 Event Notifications push events on object creation to Lambda, SQS, or SNS within seconds — event-driven and serverless. Polling adds latency and cost; FTP/EC2 and email are manual anti-patterns.

choices: S3-based data lake with Glue Data Catalog
evidence:
Data: structured, semi-structured,
unstructured. Consumers: analysts,
ML team, ad-hoc SQL. Schema: evolves.
scenarios.hint: Which architecture handles all data types with evolving schema?
scenarios.situation: Structured, semi-structured, and unstructured data serve analysts, ML, and ad-hoc SQL with evolving schemas.
scenarios.title: The lake, not the warehouse (yet)
scenarios.why: An S3-based data lake with the Glue Data Catalog stores all data types in open formats with evolving schemas, serving diverse consumers. A warehouse alone forces schema-on-write; RDS isn't analytics storage; EBS isn't a lake.

evidence:

no cluster management.
scenarios.hint: Which warehouse option scales to zero operationally for spiky use?
scenarios.situation: Petabyte-scale SQL analytics runs 2 hours/day with spikes; no cluster management wanted.
scenarios.title: A warehouse for two hours a day
scenarios.why: Redshift Serverless automatically provisions and scales warehouse capacity for the workload, paying for usage — ideal for spiky analytics. Provisioned clusters idle 22h/day; RDS isn't a warehouse; DynamoDB isn't SQL analytics.

scenarios.hint: Which service is the central metadata store queryable by Athena, Redshift, and EMR?
scenarios.situation: 500+ tables in S3; teams can't find data and schemas drift undocumented.
scenarios.title: Finding table 437
scenarios.why: The Glue Data Catalog provides a central, queryable metadata store (databases, tables, schemas, partitions) integrated with Athena, Redshift Spectrum, and EMR. Spreadsheets, hardcoded schemas, and wikis don't integrate or stay current.

evidence:
Analytics scans 10 TB/day but
queries touch 5 of 200 columns.
Need: cut scan cost.
scenarios.hint: Which format lets queries read only the columns they need?
scenarios.prompt: Which storage format cuts the scan cost?
scenarios.situation: Analytics scans 10 TB/day but queries touch only 5 of 200 columns.
scenarios.title: Reading 5 columns, not 200
scenarios.why: Parquet's columnar format lets engines read only the needed columns (plus compression and predicate pushdown), slashing scanned data and cost. Row-based CSV/JSON force full scans; plain text is worse.

evidence:
Cold data in S3 (5 PB).
Need: occasional SQL over it
without loading a warehouse.
scenarios.hint: Which Redshift feature queries S3 in place?
scenarios.prompt: What queries the cold data in place?
scenarios.situation: 5 PB of cold data in S3 needs occasional SQL without loading it into a warehouse.
scenarios.title: SQL over five petabytes, in place
scenarios.why: Redshift Spectrum extends Redshift SQL queries to S3 data in place — no loading, paying per query. Copying petabytes for occasional queries is wasteful; RDS/laptops can't handle the scale.

choices: S3 with bronze/silver/gold zones + Lake Formation permissions
evidence:
Raw events -> cleaned ->
curated marts. Need: clear lineage,
column-level access control.
scenarios.hint: Which zone pattern plus which service gives fine-grained lake security?
scenarios.prompt: What organizes the lake with proper access control?
scenarios.situation: Raw events flow to cleaned data to curated marts, needing clear lineage and column-level access control.
scenarios.title: Bronze, silver, gold
scenarios.why: Bronze/silver/gold zones organize the refinement lineage, and Lake Formation provides centralized fine-grained permissions (table/column-level) on the lake. One unstructured bucket has no lineage or control; public buckets are a breach; a single database can't hold the lake.

evidence:
Nightly ETL: 500 GB, Spark jobs.
Need: no cluster management,
auto-scaling workers.
scenarios.hint: Which service runs serverless Spark with auto-scaling?
scenarios.situation: Nightly 500 GB Spark ETL jobs need no cluster management with auto-scaling workers.
scenarios.title: Spark without the cluster
scenarios.why: AWS Glue provides serverless Spark ETL with auto-scaling workers — no clusters to manage. Self-managed EC2 reintroduces ops; Lambda can't run 4-hour Spark jobs; RDS procedures aren't a big-data engine.

evidence:
Team needs: Spark + Flink + Presto,
custom libraries, long-running
interactive notebooks.
scenarios.hint: Which service gives you a managed big-data cluster with many frameworks?
scenarios.prompt: Which service fits the multi-framework team?

evidence:
Ad-hoc SQL over S3 logs.
Usage: 10 queries/day.
Need: no infrastructure, pay per query.
scenarios.hint: Which service is serverless SQL directly on S3?
scenarios.situation: Ten ad-hoc SQL queries per day over S3 logs; no infrastructure wanted, pay per query.
scenarios.title: Ten queries a day
scenarios.why: Athena provides serverless SQL directly on S3, paying per byte scanned — perfect for low-volume ad-hoc analysis. EMR/Glue clusters idle between queries; Redshift is a provisioned warehouse.

choices: Amazon Managed Streaming for Kafka + Flink (or Kinesis Data Analytics)
evidence:
Fraud scoring: must score
transactions within 30 seconds
of occurrence.
scenarios.hint: 30-second SLA — which processing paradigm fits?
scenarios.situation: Fraud scoring must complete within 30 seconds of each transaction.
scenarios.title: Thirty seconds to score fraud
scenarios.why: Stream processing (MSK + Flink, or Kinesis Data Analytics with Flink) processes events continuously with sub-minute latency. Nightly batch, cron, and manual runs can't meet a 30-second SLA.

scenarios.hint: What tracks already-processed data so jobs handle only new arrivals?
scenarios.prompt: What stops the unbounded runtime growth?
scenarios.situation: A daily job reprocesses all 2 TB every run; runtime grows unboundedly as data accumulates.
scenarios.title: Processing everything, every day
scenarios.why: Incremental processing (e.g., Glue job bookmarks tracking processed offsets) handles only new data each run, keeping runtime flat. Full daily rewrites scale with total data; weekly reloads still reprocess; no dedup compounds the waste.

scenarios.hint: Sub-second, spiky, event-driven — which compute scales to zero?
scenarios.situation: A 200ms per-record transform is event-driven and spiky, from 0 to 10k events/sec.
scenarios.title: Two hundred milliseconds, ten thousand times
scenarios.why: Lambda scales from zero to 10k concurrent executions for short event-driven transforms with per-millisecond billing. Always-on EC2 idles at zero; EMR is for cluster analytics, not 200ms functions; bare metal is the opposite of elastic.

choices: One IAM role for all analysts
evidence:
Analysts need: sales sees all,
support sees only their region,
PII columns hidden from most.
scenarios.hint: Which service enforces column- and row-level access on the lake?
scenarios.situation: Analysts need differentiated access: full sales data for some, regional rows for support, PII columns hidden from most.
scenarios.title: Who sees which column?
scenarios.why: Lake Formation provides centralized fine-grained permissions at table, column, and row level on the data lake. Full access or one shared role can't differentiate; public buckets are a breach.

choices: AWS Glue Data Catalog + data lineage tracking
evidence:
Regulator asks: where did this
report's numbers come from?
Pipeline: 6 stages, 3 teams.
scenarios.hint: Which catalog feature traces data from source to report?
scenarios.situation: A regulator asks for the lineage of a report's numbers across a 6-stage, 3-team pipeline.
scenarios.title: Where did this number come from?
scenarios.why: The Glue Data Catalog with lineage tracking records how data flows and transforms from source to report — the auditable answer. Tribal knowledge, filenames, and no docs can't satisfy a regulator.

choices: De-identification/masking (e.g., Macie findings + masking in views)
evidence:
Analysts need realistic data.
Requirement: no real PII in
non-production environments.
scenarios.hint: What keeps data realistic while removing the sensitive values?
scenarios.prompt: What protects PII in lower environments?
scenarios.situation: Analysts need realistic data in non-production, but no real PII may exist there.
scenarios.title: Realistic, but not real
scenarios.why: De-identification and masking (finding PII with Macie, masking in views/exports) preserves analytical realism without real PII. Copying production as-is violates the requirement; trust isn't a control; deletion removes the utility.

choices: S3 Lifecycle policies aligned to retention requirements
evidence:
Regulations: 7-year retention for
financial data; 90-day for clickstream.
Volume: 3 TB/day.
scenarios.hint: Which mechanism enforces different retention per dataset automatically?
scenarios.situation: Financial data needs 7-year retention; clickstream 90 days; volume is 3 TB/day.
scenarios.title: Retention by regulation
scenarios.why: S3 Lifecycle policies enforce per-dataset retention and archival automatically at 3 TB/day scale. Keeping everything forever wastes money and may violate minimization; manual reviews don't scale; no policy is non-compliance.

choices: Deequ/Glue Data Quality rules in the pipeline with quarantine
evidence:
Bad upstream data corrupted
3 executive reports last quarter.
Need: catch it before it lands.
scenarios.hint: Which approach validates data in the pipeline and quarantines failures?
scenarios.prompt: What catches bad data before it lands?
scenarios.situation: Bad upstream data corrupted executive reports; quality must be enforced before data lands.
scenarios.title: Trust, but verify the data
scenarios.why: Data quality rules (e.g., Glue Data Quality / Deequ checks) in the pipeline validate schema, completeness, and ranges, quarantining failures before they corrupt downstream. Eyeballing and post-ship fixes are the current failure; no checks guarantees repeats.

choices: Data mesh principles: domain ownership + data products with contracts
A single central team doing everything
evidence:
8 domains, 40 engineers.
Central team is the bottleneck.
Need: scale data ownership.
scenarios.hint: Which paradigm distributes ownership to domains with contracts?
scenarios.situation: Eight domains and 40 engineers; the central data team is the bottleneck.
scenarios.title: Beyond the central bottleneck
scenarios.why: Data mesh distributes ownership to domain teams who publish data products with contracts/SLAs, scaling ownership with the organization. A central-everything team is the current bottleneck; one giant database doesn't distribute ownership; emailed CSVs aren't governance.

choices: Amazon MWAA (Managed Workflows for Apache Airflow)
evidence:
Pipeline: 50 tasks, dependencies,
retries, SLAs. Team knows Airflow.
Need: managed service.
scenarios.hint: Which managed service runs Airflow?
scenarios.situation: A 50-task pipeline with dependencies, retries, and SLAs; the team knows Airflow and wants it managed.
scenarios.title: Fifty tasks, one DAG
scenarios.why: MWAA provides managed Apache Airflow — DAGs with dependencies, retries, and SLA monitoring without managing the orchestrator. Single-EC2 cron is a single point of failure; manual runs don't scale; Lambda alone lacks DAG orchestration semantics.

evidence:
Workflow: ingest -> validate ->
transform -> load -> notify.
Need: visual workflow, retries,
error handling per step.
scenarios.hint: Which serverless service orchestrates steps with visual workflows and built-in error handling?
scenarios.situation: A 5-step workflow needs visual monitoring, per-step retries, and error handling.
scenarios.title: Steps with a safety net
scenarios.why: Step Functions orchestrates serverless workflows with visual execution graphs, per-state retries/catches, and integrations to Lambda, Glue, and more. Manual Lambda chaining reinvents error handling; one giant Lambda couples everything; bash on EC2 is fragile.

choices: Event-driven triggers (S3 events, EventBridge) + idempotent tasks
evidence:
Files arrive unpredictably.
Need: pipeline starts on arrival,
handles duplicates safely.
scenarios.hint: What starts work on arrival and survives duplicate events?
scenarios.situation: Files arrive unpredictably; the pipeline must start on arrival and handle duplicate events safely.
scenarios.title: Start when the file lands
scenarios.why: Event-driven triggers (S3 Event Notifications, EventBridge) start pipelines on arrival with low latency, and idempotent tasks make duplicate events safe. Fixed schedules add latency; polling wastes resources; manual triggers don't scale.

choices: Dead-letter queues + alerting + backoff with jitter
evidence:
Task fails intermittently.
Current: infinite immediate retries
thundering the downstream.
scenarios.hint: What handles failure gracefully without hammering downstream?
scenarios.situation: Intermittent task failures trigger infinite immediate retries that thunder the downstream service.
scenarios.title: The retry thundering herd
scenarios.why: Backoff with jitter spreads retries, DLQs isolate persistent failures for inspection, and alerting notifies humans — graceful degradation instead of a retry storm. Blind infinite retries are the current failure; ignoring/deleting loses data.

choices: One pipeline for dev and prod
Separate dev/staging/prod with promotion of tested artifacts
evidence:
Pipeline changes broke prod.
Need: test changes safely,
promote what works.
scenarios.hint: What keeps experiments out of production?
scenarios.prompt: What prevents the next prod breakage?
scenarios.situation: Pipeline changes broke production; changes need safe testing and promotion.
scenarios.title: Don't develop in production
scenarios.why: Separate environments with promotion of tested artifacts (code, not just data) let changes prove themselves before production. One shared pipeline couples experiments to prod; developing in prod is the current failure.

choices: CloudWatch + pipeline-native monitoring with SLA alerts
evidence:
SLA: data ready by 6 AM.
Need: alert if any upstream
task risks the SLA.
scenarios.hint: What watches every task against the deadline, not just the end?
scenarios.situation: Data must be ready by 6 AM; the team needs alerts when any upstream task risks the SLA.
scenarios.title: Data by 6 AM, guaranteed
scenarios.why: Pipeline-native monitoring (Airflow SLAs, Step Functions/CloudWatch alarms on task duration) watches every task against the deadline and alerts early. Manual checks and output-only monitoring detect misses too late; no monitoring is blindness.

evidence:
200 business users need
interactive dashboards over the
warehouse. No BI infrastructure.

scenarios.situation: 200 business users need interactive dashboards over the warehouse with no BI infrastructure to manage.
scenarios.title: Dashboards for two hundred users
scenarios.why: QuickSight provides managed BI with SPICE in-memory engine, integrating natively with AWS data sources and scaling to hundreds of users. Custom builds reintroduce ops; email chains and screenshots aren't BI.

choices: Moving data to the ML platform
SageMaker Canvas / ML in SQL (Redshift ML)

Analysts know SQL, not Python.
Need: churn predictions from
warehouse data, quickly.
scenarios.hint: Which options let SQL users build models without moving data?
scenarios.situation: SQL-fluent analysts need churn predictions from warehouse data without learning Python or moving data.
scenarios.title: Machine learning in SQL
scenarios.why: Redshift ML and SageMaker Canvas let analysts build and use models with SQL or no-code interfaces against warehouse data in place. Moving data adds pipelines; laptop training doesn't scale; gut feeling isn't ML.

choices: Apache Hudi/Iceberg-style table formats on S3 (upserts, time travel)
Keeping every version as separate files
A relational database for the lake
evidence:
Lake table: 10B rows.
Need: upserts/deletes and
time-travel queries on S3.
scenarios.hint: Which open table formats bring warehouse features to S3?
scenarios.prompt: What enables upserts and time travel on the lake?
scenarios.situation: A 10B-row lake table needs upserts, deletes, and time-travel queries on S3.
scenarios.title: Upserts on the data lake

choices: Caching in the BI tool only
evidence:
Dashboard queries scan 2 TB
each load. 500 loads/day.
Same aggregations repeatedly.
scenarios.hint: What precomputes the repeated aggregations?
scenarios.prompt: What cuts the repeated 2 TB scans?
scenarios.situation: Dashboards repeatedly scan 2 TB for the same aggregations, 500 times a day.
scenarios.title: Scanning two terabytes, five hundred times
scenarios.why: Materialized views or scheduled aggregation tables precompute the repeated aggregations once, so dashboards read megabytes instead of terabytes. One-off queries repeat the waste; bigger warehouses just scan faster at higher cost; BI-only caching is fragile.

choices: Row/column-level security in the BI and lake layers
evidence:
Requirement: managers see only
their region's data in dashboards.
scenarios.hint: Which security feature filters rows by viewer?
scenarios.situation: Dashboard viewers must see only their own region's data.
scenarios.title: Your region, your numbers
scenarios.why: Row-level (and column-level) security in QuickSight and Lake Formation filters data by viewer identity — enforced, not advisory. Full access violates the requirement; one shared dashboard can't differentiate; trust isn't enforcement.

choices: Cost allocation tags + query-level cost attribution (e.g., Athena workgroups, Redshift concurrency scaling) + lifecycle policies
evidence:
Analytics bill tripled.
Nobody knows which team or
workload caused it.
scenarios.hint: What attributes analytics spend to teams and workloads?
scenarios.prompt: What brings the analytics spend under control?
scenarios.situation: The analytics bill tripled with no attribution to teams or workloads.
scenarios.title: The tripled analytics bill
scenarios.why: Cost allocation tags plus query-level attribution (Athena workgroups with per-workgroup limits, Redshift usage tracking) identify who spent what, and lifecycle policies curb storage growth. A single undivided bill can't be managed; ignoring it repeats the tripling.

lessons.title: Data Ingestion — Core concepts
concepts: Kinesis Data Streams provides ordered, replayable, high-throughput streaming with multiple consumers per shard. Kinesis Data Firehose is the managed delivery service: it buffers, converts (e.g., to Parquet), and loads streaming data into S3 and other destinations with no consumer code.

Streaming ingestion: SQS is queue-based (not replayable multi-consumer streaming); S3 batch uploads aren't sub-second; RDS isn't an ingestion service. Data Streams and MSK require consumers; DynamoDB direct PUT isn't a streaming pipeline.
Firehose/Data Streams aren't Kafka-compatible; SQS FIFO lacks Kafka's log semantics and retention model.

Managed delivery: amazon MSK provides managed Apache Kafka with Kafka API compatibility, configurable long retention, and exactly-once semantics support. AWS Transfer Family provides managed SFTP/FTPS/FTP endpoints backed by S3 — partners keep their workflow, files land in S3.

ML for analysts: redshift ML and SageMaker Canvas let analysts build and use models with SQL or no-code interfaces against warehouse data in place.
Open table formats (Apache Hudi, Iceberg — supported by Athena, EMR, Glue) bring upserts, deletes, and time travel to S3 data lakes.
Materialized views or scheduled aggregation tables precompute the repeated aggregations once, so dashboards read megabytes instead of terabytes.

example.code:
Requirement: managers see only
their region's data in dashboards.
example.walkthrough: Row-level (and column-level) security in QuickSight and Lake Formation filters data by viewer identity — enforced, not advisory. Full access violates the requirement; one shared dashboard can't differentiate; trust isn't enforcement.

pitfalls: Common trap: materialized views / scheduled aggregations.
Common trap: cost allocation tags + query-level cost attribution (e.g., Athena workgroups, Redshift concurrency scaling) + lifecycle policies.
Common trap: keeping every version as separate files.
Common trap: building custom dashboards from scratch.

lessons.title: AWS Data Analytics — Core concepts
concepts: Design around the analytics flow: ingest (Kinesis for streaming, batch loads for scheduled), store (S3 data lake in open formats), catalog (Glue Data Catalog as the shared metadata layer), process (Glue/EMR), and consume (Athena for ad-hoc, Redshift for heavy BI, QuickSight for dashboards).

The data lake's economics live in file layout: partition by time or key, store as Parquet/ORC with compression, and avoid the small-files problem. These choices decide whether Athena queries cost cents or dollars.

Streaming systems scale on keys and shards: Kinesis throughput is per-shard, so high-cardinality partition keys and right-sized shard counts are the design levers; Firehose fits delivery-to-destination streaming without consumer management.

Choose the query engine by pattern: Athena for serverless ad-hoc SQL on S3, Redshift (provisioned or Serverless) for complex joins at warehouse scale, EMR for Spark-scale transformations and ML preprocessing. One engine rarely serves all three well.

Build pipelines that heal: Glue job bookmarks for idempotent retries, dead-letter routing for malformed records, schema evolution in the catalog, and alerts on repeated failure rather than on every hiccup.

example.code:
aws athena start-query-execution \
  --query-string "SELECT event_type, count(*) FROM clicks WHERE year='2026' AND month='10' GROUP BY 1" \
  --query-execution-context Database=weblogs --result-configuration OutputLocation=s3://results-bucket/athena/
example.walkthrough: A serverless SQL query against partitioned S3 data — no cluster involved. The WHERE clause on partition columns (year, month) is what keeps Athena from scanning the whole dataset, which is the difference between a cheap query and an expensive one.

pitfalls: Common trap: querying unpartitioned CSV in Athena and paying to scan terabytes for a megabyte answer — partition and use Parquet.
Common trap: low-cardinality Kinesis partition keys — one hot shard throttles the whole stream regardless of shard count.
Common trap: treating the data lake as a file dump with no catalog — undocumented data is undead data; crawl it into the Glue Data Catalog.
Common trap: no job bookmarks on Glue ETL — every retry reprocesses everything and duplicates output.

simulations.title: Wire the nightly ETL
simulations.brief: The warehouse refresh runs nightly. Order the pipeline stages so each step reads complete upstream output.

steps.context: Nightly ETL: extract from sources, transform, load the warehouse, then validate.
items: Transform and clean the extracted records
Validate row counts and publish the data-quality report
Extract changed records from the source systems
Load the transformed data into the warehouse

simulations.debrief: You ordered the ETL correctly: extract, transform, load, then validate. Validation last means the report covers the whole run.

simulations.title: The warehouse is stale
simulations.brief: The 06:00 warehouse refresh never landed and the dashboard shows yesterday's numbers. The orchestrator log is your evidence.

steps.symptom: Warehouse tables are 24h stale; the orchestrator shows the extract stage green, transform red.
evidence:
extract: 1.2M rows staged to s3://ilb-data-raw ... OK
transform: ERROR schema mismatch on column 'amount' (expected INTEGER, got TEXT)
load: skipped (upstream failed)
options: Re-run the whole pipeline — transient errors clear on retry
Inspect the raw staged data: the source changed the 'amount' column type
Drop the warehouse table and reload from scratch
Disable the transform stage so the load can proceed
steps.explain: The log names it: a schema mismatch on 'amount'. The source changed the column type — re-running or skipping transform just repeats or hides the failure. Fix the schema handling first.

steps.symptom: The source now sends 'amount' as TEXT ('2400' instead of 2400).
options: Cast TEXT to INTEGER in the transform with validation for bad values
Change the warehouse column to TEXT to match the source
Ask the source team to revert — pipelines should never adapt
Load the TEXT values and fix them in the dashboard queries
steps.explain: Adapt in the transform with explicit casting and bad-value handling — that is what the transform stage is for. Changing the warehouse type corrupts downstream analytics; dashboard-side fixes hide the problem.

simulations.debrief: You diagnosed a schema-drift failure at the right layer: the transform adapts and validates, the warehouse stays clean, and the evidence led every step.

simulations.title: Schema-on-write or schema-on-read?
simulations.brief: The team argues about where to enforce schema: at ingest (strict) or at read (flexible). The workload decides — walk the tree.

steps.text: The new clickstream feed arrives as messy JSON, fields change weekly, and analysts explore it ad hoc. Enforce schema at ingest?

choices.label: Yes — strict schema at ingest keeps everything clean
choices.feedback: Strict ingest schema on a weekly-changing feed means the pipeline breaks weekly. Flexibility matters here.

choices.label: No — land it raw, enforce schema at read time
choices.feedback: Correct — schema-on-read (data lake pattern) absorbs volatile feeds without breaking ingest.

steps.text: The pipeline broke twice this month on new fields. Reconsider:

choices.label: Land raw, enforce at read
choices.feedback: Right — let the lake be flexible and push structure to query time.

steps.text: Now the finance ledger: regulated, audited, downstream reports must reconcile to the cent. Same choice?

choices.label: Schema-on-read again — consistency
choices.feedback: Wrong: regulated financial data needs schema-on-write with validation at ingest. Flexibility here is a compliance violation.

choices.label: Schema-on-write with validation — it is regulated data
choices.feedback: Correct — the workload decides. Volatile exploration data gets schema-on-read; regulated data gets strict schema-on-write.

simulations.debrief: You learned the real rule: there is no single right answer — volatile exploration data wants schema-on-read, regulated data demands schema-on-write.

simulations.title: The crawler that misfires
simulations.brief: The Glue crawler keeps creating a new table per file instead of one table per dataset. Review the crawler config and click the offending lines.

steps.config:
Crawler: nightly-raw-crawl
1. S3 path: s3://ilb-data-raw/
2. Table prefix: raw_
3. Schema change policy: update table
4. Partition detection: disabled
5. Schedule: cron(0 2 * * ? *)

issues.description: Crawling the whole bucket root mixes datasets with different schemas into conflicting table definitions.
issues.fix: Point the crawler at one dataset prefix per crawler (e.g. s3://ilb-data-raw/clickstream/).

issues.description: Partition detection disabled means date-partitioned data crawls as separate tables.
issues.fix: Enable partition detection so partitions map to one table.

simulations.debrief: You found the crawler misconfiguration: scope the path per dataset and let partition detection do its job. One dataset, one table.

sections.heading: Data Ingestion
items: Kinesis Data Streams — provides ordered, replayable, high-throughput streaming with multiple consumers per shard. Kinesis Data Firehose is the managed delivery service: it buffers, converts (e.g., to Parquet), and loads streaming data into S3 and other destinations with no consum…

Streaming ingestion — SQS is queue-based (not replayable multi-consumer streaming); S3 batch uploads aren't sub-second; RDS isn't an ingestion service. Data Streams and MSK require consumers; DynamoDB direct PUT isn't a streaming pipeline.
Firehose — Firehose/Data Streams aren't Kafka-compatible; SQS FIFO lacks Kafka's log semantics and retention model.

Managed delivery — amazon MSK provides managed Apache Kafka with Kafka API compatibility, configurable long retention, and exactly-once semantics support. AWS Transfer Family provides managed SFTP/FTPS/FTP endpoints backed by S3 — partners keep their workflow, files land in S3.
Common trap — kinesis Data Streams with custom consumers.
Skipping the key question — which service is built for high-throughput ordered event streams with multiple consumers.
Skipping the key question — which service loads streaming data to destinations with no consumer code.

Kinesis Data Streams — provides ordered, replayable, high-throughput streaming with multiple consumers per shard. SQS is queue-based (not replayable multi-consumer streaming); S3 batch uploads aren't sub-second; RDS isn't an ingestion service.

sections.heading: Data Lakes & Warehouses
items: Data lakes — an S3-based data lake with the Glue Data Catalog stores all data types in open formats with evolving schemas, serving diverse consumers. The Glue Data Catalog provides a central, queryable metadata store (databases, tables, schemas, partitions) integrated w…
S3 — S3: redshift Spectrum extends Redshift SQL queries to S3 data in place — no loading, paying per query.
Redshift Serverless — Redshift Serverless automatically provisions and scales warehouse capacity for the workload, paying for usage — ideal for spiky analytics.
Glue Data Catalog — parquet's columnar format lets engines read only the needed columns (plus compression and predicate pushdown), slashing scanned data and cost.
Common trap — S3 with bronze/silver/gold zones + Lake Formation permissions.
Skipping the key question — which architecture handles all data types with evolving schema.
Skipping the key question — which warehouse option scales to zero operationally for spiky use.

An S3-based — An S3-based data lake with the Glue Data Catalog stores all data types in open formats with evolving schemas, serving diverse consumers. A warehouse alone forces schema-on-write; RDS isn't analytics storage; EBS isn't a lake.

sections.heading: Processing Frameworks
items: Glue — is Spark-centric serverless; Lambda isn't for clusters; Athena is serverless SQL, not a framework platform. Incremental processing (e.g., Glue job bookmarks tracking processed offsets) handles only new data each run, keeping runtime flat.

Serverless Spark — AWS Glue provides serverless Spark ETL with auto-scaling workers — no clusters to manage. EMR provides managed clusters with the full big-data ecosystem (Spark, Flink, Presto/Trino) and notebook support.

EMR — always-on EC2 idles at zero; EMR is for cluster analytics, not 200ms functions; bare metal is the opposite of elastic. EMR/Glue clusters idle between queries; Redshift is a provisioned warehouse.

Big data clusters — stream processing (MSK + Flink, or Kinesis Data Analytics with Flink) processes events continuously with sub-minute latency. Full daily rewrites scale with total data; weekly reloads still reprocess; no dedup compounds the waste.
Athena — provides serverless SQL directly on S3, paying per byte scanned — perfect for low-volume ad-hoc analysis.
Common trap — amazon Managed Streaming for Kafka + Flink (or Kinesis Data Analytics).
Skipping the key question — which service runs serverless Spark with auto-scaling.
Skipping the key question — which service gives you a managed big-data cluster with many frameworks.

Lambda — Lambda scales from zero to 10k concurrent executions for short event-driven transforms with per-millisecond billing. Always-on EC2 idles at zero; EMR is for cluster analytics, not 200ms functions; bare metal is the opposite of elastic.

sections.heading: Data Governance
items: Lake Formation — provides centralized fine-grained permissions at table, column, and row level on the data lake.
Fine-grained access — full access or one shared role can't differentiate; public buckets are a breach.

Data lineage — the Glue Data Catalog with lineage tracking records how data flows and transforms from source to report — the auditable answer. Data mesh distributes ownership to domain teams who publish data products with contracts/SLAs, scaling ownership with the organiz…
PII handling — de-identification and masking (finding PII with Macie, masking in views/exports) preserves analytical realism without real PII.
Data — Data quality rules (e.g., Glue Data Quality / Deequ checks) in the pipeline validate schema, completeness, and ranges, quarantining failures before they corrupt downstream.
Common trap — data mesh principles: domain ownership + data products with contracts.
Common trap — lake Formation fine-grained permissions (table/column/row level).
Common trap — S3 Lifecycle policies aligned to retention requirements.
Common trap — everyone gets full access.

S3 Lifecycle — S3 Lifecycle policies enforce per-dataset retention and archival automatically at 3 TB/day scale. Keeping everything forever wastes money and may violate minimization; manual reviews don't scale; no policy is non-compliance.

sections.heading: Orchestration
items: MWAA provides managed Apache Airflow — DAGs with dependencies, retries, and SLA monitoring without managing the orchestrator.

checklist: Get 7–8 hours of sleep the night before — fatigue destroys recall faster than any topic gap.
Bring valid government-issued photo ID and arrive at the test center 30 minutes early.
Eat a real meal beforehand; bring water and a light snack if the center allows them.
Read every question twice before scanning the answer choices.
Flag uncertain questions and move on — return with fresh eyes at the end.
Eliminate the obviously wrong answers first, then compare the survivors.
Budget your time: answer steadily and keep a 10–15 minute review buffer.
Re-run your weakest-domain drill until mastery is at least 80%.
For Data Ingestion: restate the 'why' behind each scenario answer in your own words — if you can't explain it, you don't own it.
Redo one Data Lakes & Warehouses lab from scratch without looking at the steps.
Recite the key Processing Frameworks terms from the glossary aloud from memory.
